name: PT Famon Awal Bros Sedaya Tbk

frontmatter.title: Primaya Hospital — a good network at a konglo price
frontmatter.summary: Primaya runs one of the larger listed private hospital networks in Indonesia and is still adding capacity. The operating story is credible; the cash conversion is not, because capex absorbs most of the EBITDA the network earns. On our cash flows the shares are worth far less than the price, and only a very small float keeps the premium alive. We initiate at Reduce.
thesis: The network is the real thing. Revenue rose from IDR1,522.6bn in FY2022A to IDR2,436.8bn in FY2025A, with 20.0 hospitals, more than 3,000 beds and growing inpatient and outpatient volumes [[S0]][[S8]].

FY2026 is an earnings trough, not a margin one. EBITDA grows inside the company's own 20.0% to 25.0% projection and the EBITDA margin ends flat, but depreciation on the new estate and interest on the debt that built it take earnings per share down -5.0% in FY2026E [[S6]][[S8]]; the margin we model never exceeds the FY2025A level.

Cash conversion is the constraint. Capex ran at 35.5% of revenue in FY2025A and free cash flow to the firm was IDR-266.6bn [[S7]]; the dividend is nil [[S8]]. Value depends on that capex ratio falling as the build-out matures.
The price is not a forecast of growth. The discounted cash flow is worth Rp184 per share against a price of Rp715, and the blended fundamental value before the konglo lens is Rp535 [[S0]].
The float is the swing factor. Free float of 7.9% must reach 12.5% by 31 March 2027, 4.5 months away, and the name left the IHSG calculation on 13 November 2026 [[S25]].
We initiate at REDUCE with a twelve-month target of Rp609, a -14.8% total return - the cash flows say sell, the ownership regime says the premium closes slowly rather than at once.

blocks.text: We initiate PT Famon Awal Bros Sedaya (Primaya Hospital) at **REDUCE** with a twelve-month target of Rp609, a -14.8% total return from the Rp715 last print of 13 November 2026 [[S0]], and no dividend [[S8]]. The target is not a fundamental value. Our fundamental twelve-month value after the house liquidity discount is Rp374, and the target sits above it only because the konglo lens assumes that a controller-dominated float gives up part of its premium over twelve months rather than all of it at once. On the cash flows alone the answer is harsher: the discounted-cash-flow leg is worth Rp184 per share.

The business is not the problem. Primaya is one of the larger listed private hospital networks in Indonesia by bed count, with 20.0 hospitals and more than 3,000 beds at end-2025 [[S8]], a middle-to-upper income franchise built around cardiac, cancer, neuroscience and mother-and-child centres [[S8]], and a record of turning a small regional group into a national network [[S9]]. Revenue compounded from IDR1,522.6bn in FY2022A to IDR2,436.8bn in FY2025A [[S0]][[S7]], and first-half 2026 revenue of IDR1,432.7bn grew well ahead of the guidance range the company had set for itself [[S6]][[S8]]. Inpatient days and outpatient visits both rose in 2025, with outpatient growth the faster of the two [[S8]].

What the market pays for that is the question. At Rp715 the shares sit on 49.7x our FY2026E earnings and 18.0x our FY2026E EBITDA [[S0]], for a company whose earnings per share we expect to fall -5.0% in FY2026E as new capacity depreciates before it earns [[S6]]. The premium is not a forecast of superior growth. It is what a 7.9% free float does to the marginal price: the controller vehicles and the founder hold the rest [[S8]]. The pack reports three-month traded value of 25,924,563.5 a day [[S0]], which at Rp715 works out at only about thirty-six thousand shares - the signature of a lot-based volume multiplied by price rather than rupiah - so the honest order of magnitude is nearer three billion rupiah a day. We cannot correct that pack field here, and we do not need to: the house liquidity discount of 0.3 is a lens parameter applied to a 7.9% float, not a number fitted to the turnover, and no target rests on it. Since 13 November 2026 the stock has been outside the IHSG calculation as a high-shareholding- concentration name [[S25]].

Three things move the value. First, whether capex really falls from the FY2025A 35.5% of revenue toward the mid-teens, because that single line separates a cash-consuming build-out from a cash-generating network. Second, whether the 2026 gross-margin trough recovers as Kelapa Gading and the newly managed hospitals mature [[S6]]. Third, the free-float deadline of 31 March 2027, which forces a controller decision inside 4.5 months [[S25]]. The first two are fundamental and are in the model; the third is a regime event that sets the path of the share price without changing the value of the business.

The variant view is therefore split, and deliberately so. Against the cash flows we are well below the price and the rating would be harsher than Reduce. Against the ownership regime we are above the fundamental value, because a stock with a float this small and a controller with no forced seller does not re-rate to fair value on our forecast horizon. Reduce is the honest blend of the two.

Primaya Hospital Group is an Indonesian private hospital operator. At end-2025 it owned and/or managed 20.0 hospitals with more than 3,000 beds, having grown from a regional base in Batam and Bekasi into a national network [[S8]][[S9]]. It runs a middle-to-upper income model built on centres of excellence in cardiac and vascular, cancer, neuroscience, urology and nephrology, orthopaedics and sports medicine, diabetes and metabolic disease, and mother and child, supported by clinical laboratories, homecare, medical evacuation and a round-the-clock emergency service [[S8]]. Revenue comes from patients, private insurers and the national health scheme; no single customer is material to the group [[S7]].

The revenue mix inside the hospital business is disclosed in some detail, and it matters for margin analysis. The notes split inpatient medical support, outpatient medical support, inpatient services, laboratory, polyclinic services, medical equipment sales and other revenue [[S7]]. The support and laboratory lines carry the drugs, consumables and equipment; the room lines carry the building, the beds and the depreciation. A shift in mix toward the medical support lines therefore raises both revenue and cost at the same time, which is why the consolidated gross margin of 28.0% in FY2025A can fall to 26.6% in a year of capacity addition without any change in pricing [[S7]][[S6]].

Geographically the group reports Java, Kalimantan and Sulawesi, and Sumatera. Java carries the largest revenue share and the strongest operating margin in the segment note, Kalimantan and Sulawesi sit above Sumatera, and Sumatera is the newest and thinnest market at the operating line [[S7]]. That is the shape of a network that built out from its Jakarta and Kalimantan base into territory where brand and doctor density are still being established: the newest sites carry the ramp cost, and the segment note shows it plainly.

The operating strategy is stated without ambiguity. Management targets new hospital openings on a fixed annual cadence, funded from operating cash and debt, and surrounds the hospitals with an ecosystem of subsidiaries spanning clinical laboratories, fertility and eye clinics, hospital information systems, telemedicine, medical devices, a training centre and a health education institution [[S8]][[S9]]. The most recent cycle brought Kelapa Gading in North Jakarta, a large flagship with international-standard centres of excellence, plus the hospitals acquired and brought under management through PT Jala Mas Putra Rejeki [[S6]][[S8]]. The acquisitions are visible in the accounts: goodwill and intangibles rose, non-controlling interests appeared in the acquired hospital companies, and the depreciation charge stepped up as the acquired assets came onto the consolidated balance sheet [[S7]].

Position in the market: with over 3,000 beds Primaya sits behind the largest listed networks and ahead of the single-city operators, and it competes for the same middle-income patient as the other listed groups. It is a challenger, not the leader. Its edge is regional density in Kalimantan and the outer islands, where it built early, plus a Jakarta flagship aimed at the international-patient and medical-tourism segment the government has been promoting [[S8]][[S9]]. Management frames the strategy as a move from hospital care to a healthcare ecosystem, with medical tourism as the growth narrative [[S9]].

Ownership is founder-led rather than conglomerate-led. PT Famon Obor Maju holds 46.5%, Archipelago Investment Pte Ltd 27.1%, PT Awal Bros Citra Batam 17.3%, Professor Yos Effendi Susanto personally 0.8%, and the public 8.2% of the shares [[S8]]. The founder has been building hospitals since 1988 and co-founded the Mitra Keluarga group before Primaya [[S8]]. The group employed 7,352.0 people at the last count [[S0]]. The governance section sets out what that ownership means for a minority holder.

Indonesian private hospitals sell capacity, doctors and trust. Demand comes from demographics, urbanisation, the growth of the insured middle class, the expansion of the national health scheme and the medical-tourism ambition the government has pushed since the pandemic, and the industry bodies describe that demand as the reason the scheme itself depends on private providers [[S10]][[S11]]. Supply is constrained by specialist doctor numbers, licensing, accreditation and capital: a hospital is a multi-year, capital-heavy project whose fixed cost base arrives before its patients [[S8]]. That asymmetry, not the demand growth, is what determines returns.

The regulation that matters most is the class-standard rule for national-health inpatients, which replaces the room-class structure with a single facilities standard and has been applied from 2025 with the scheme's own class structure re-cut since [[S11]]. For a private operator it cuts both ways: it standardises what a national-scheme bed must contain, which raises the capital cost of serving that segment, and it removes some of the room-class differentiation that private hospitals used to sell. The second regulatory thread is accreditation and patient safety, which the health ministry has been reworking alongside the scheme's benefit package [[S10]]. The industry's own associations have been explicit that the viability of the national scheme depends on private hospitals, which serve the majority of its participants, and that those hospitals face regulatory, financing and digital-transformation pressure at the same time [[S11]]. The finance ministry has been in the same conversation, which tells you the tariff question is fiscal, not clinical [[S10]].

The competitive landscape is a set of listed networks and a long tail of single-site and two-site hospitals. Competition is local: patients choose on distance, doctor, specialty and payer acceptance, not on group brand. The moat in this industry is therefore doctor density, clinical reputation in a specialty, payer contracts and fixed-cost absorption through occupancy. Primaya's own numbers show how thin that moat is at the margin. A 28.0% gross margin in FY2025A fell to 26.6% on our FY2026E as new beds opened [[S7]][[S6]], because a new hospital carries consultants, nurses, equipment and depreciation from its first day and fills over several years. A group that opens hospitals on a fixed annual cadence permanently carries a cohort of ramping assets, so its consolidated margin is structurally below its mature-site margin. That is not a management failure; it is the arithmetic of the model.

Five forces, briefly. Buyer power is high and rising where the national scheme sets tariffs and private insurers negotiate case rates. Supplier power is high in specialist doctors and imported devices, and the rupiah at Rp18,190/USD to the dollar against Rp18,350/USD forecast keeps imported consumable costs in focus: a weaker rupiah raises the cost of drugs and devices with no offset in tariffs. The threat of new entrants is moderate, because capital and licensing are real barriers but regional competitors are numerous and every mid-sized city has a credible second entrant. Substitutes are public hospitals and out-of-country care for the top of the market. Rivalry among the listed networks is intensifying as each adds beds into the same urban catchments [[S11]][[S7]].

External influences we carry into the model are the currency path above, the policy rate at 5.8 rate (the group carries IDR1,932.1bn of debt against IDR735.9bn of cash at end-2025, so refinancing cost is a real line rather than a rounding item) [[S7]], and the consumer backdrop, which the company itself named as a 2025 headwind alongside health-policy change and higher operating costs [[S8]]. The operating drivers that matter for a hospital - bed additions, occupancy, case mix and payer mix - all move in the same direction as those three, which is why we model revenue from bed count and volume from the company's own disclosed inpatient days and outpatient visits [[S8]] rather than from a sector forecast.

Our industry view is that this is a structurally growing sector with a capital-intensity problem at the individual-hospital level. The hospital that is full earns good returns; the hospital that is ramping does not. An investor buying the consolidated group is buying a blend of both, and the blend is worth a lower multiple than the mature assets alone would command. That is a reason to own hospitals selectively and a reason to be careful about paying a growth multiple for a consolidated number that includes the ramp [[S7]][[S8]].

Market share is not disclosed in a way we can source, so we do not claim a figure. What is sourced is the shape: a growing network with a national footprint, a flagship in the capital, and a segment note showing one region still below group margin [[S7]][[S8]]. On the evidence we hold, Primaya is a credible challenger with a defensible regional franchise and no durable pricing power against the payer.

**History.** Revenue rose from IDR1,522.6bn in FY2022A [[S0]] through IDR1,839.2bn in FY2023A [[S8]] and IDR2,103.1bn to IDR2,436.8bn in FY2025A, 15.9% in the last year [[S7]]. Gross margin reached 28.0%, operating expenses were IDR410.7bn or about a sixth of revenue, and operating profit was IDR270.5bn [[S7]]. The line the data pack gets wrong is depreciation: the audited notes charge IDR253.6bn of fixed-asset depreciation split between cost of revenues and operating expenses, against a figure of only a few billion in the pack [[S7]]. Restating it lifts EBITDA to IDR524.1bn, a 21.5% margin, and that restated history is what the forecast is built on. EBITDA is the right yardstick for a hospital because the asset base is the business; EBIT moves with the age of the estate.

**The 2026 shape.** First-half 2026 revenue was IDR1,432.7bn, with depreciation of IDR163.0bn against a far smaller charge a year earlier as the new assets came on line, profit before tax of IDR105.3bn and profit attributable to shareholders of IDR58.6bn [[S6]]. Gross margin fell to well below the FY2025A level, operating margin compressed with it, and the effective tax rate in the half ran above the statutory rate [[S6]]. This is the trough we model through rather than a trend we extrapolate. FY2026E revenue of IDR2,948.6bn is 21.0% growth, above the company's 15.0% to 20.0% projection band - a band the first half already outgrew, so we hold the second half at the group's ordinary mid-teens pace rather than at the first-half rate. FY2026E EBITDA of IDR631.0bn against IDR524.1bn in FY2025A sits inside the company's 20.0% to 25.0% EBITDA projection [[S8]], at a 21.4% margin against 21.5% in FY2025A [[S0]]: the guide is met by revenue and a flat margin, not by an assumed margin gain.

**Margins.** We model gross margin of 26.6% in FY2026E, recovering steadily to 26.8% by FY2030E - still below the FY2025A level, because the recovery is new hospitals filling, not price. Operating expenses are held flat at 16.4% of revenue through FY2030E, the ratio the first half of 2026 actually delivered on a IDR1,432.7bn revenue base [[S6]]; we assume no operating leverage at all, because the two prior years moved the ratio up, not down [[S7]], and there is no disclosed fixed-cost study to support more. The result is an EBITDA margin that runs from 21.4% to 21.5% - flat against the 21.5% of FY2025A, not a recovery to a better one. The only margin history we can compare with is FY2024A-FY2025A, at 22.1% and 21.5% on D&A restated from the filings [[S7]]; the FY2023A EBITDA line in the model still carries the data pack's depreciation and is not a usable comparison, a gap we flag rather than smooth over.

**Cash flow and capex.** This is where the investment case lives. Capex was IDR864.2bn in FY2025A, 35.5% of revenue, and free cash flow to the firm was IDR-266.6bn [[S7]]. The first half of 2026 shows the turn: fixed-asset spending and advances fell by well over half against the same period a year earlier [[S6]], and the end-2025 balance sheet carried substantial construction in progress that converts into operating assets without new cash [[S8]]. We model capex at 15.0% of revenue in FY2026E, rising to 17.0% as the next sites are built, then fading to 15.0% by FY2030E and below that in the long run, with free cash flow to the firm of IDR44.4bn in FY2026E and IDR32.0bn in FY2028E. The capex path is the whole valuation, so it is worth stating exactly what happens if it does not happen. Held at the FY2025A ratio of 35.5% of revenue - IDR864.2bn in FY2025A - capex alone would exceed the EBITDA the group earns each year (IDR631.0bn in FY2026E), free cash flow to the firm would be negative from the first forecast year to the last, and the DCF equity value would not halve: it would turn negative, by more than the enterprise value the method produces at our modelled path. That is not a stress we carry in the base case; it is the reason the capex assumption is the one line we would challenge first in a review.

**Balance sheet and debt.** Net debt was IDR1,196.2bn at end-2025, 2.3 times EBITDA, with IDR1,932.1bn of debt against IDR735.9bn of cash [[S7]]. Debt rose through the build-out and the acquisitions. We assume no net new borrowing and fund the programme from operating cash, with net debt to EBITDA easing to 1.9 in FY2026E. Covenant headroom is not disclosed in the filings we hold, which is itself a monitoring item; the company's own projection targets a debt-to-equity ratio and a debt-to-assets ratio below one [[S8]], and our forecast stays comfortably inside both.

**Capital allocation.** No dividend has been paid to shareholders of the parent since the listing: the statements of changes in equity and the cash-flow statements show dividends only to non-controlling interests in subsidiaries, and the company's projection for 2026 carries no dividend line [[S7]][[S8]]. Every rupiah of operating cash goes into the opening programme. That is defensible for a network still adding capacity, but it means shareholder return has to come from the value of the assets built rather than from distributions, and it removes the yield support that would otherwise cushion a de-rating.

**Earnings quality.** The accrual picture is not the problem: profit tracks cash once depreciation is added back, and the group has no history of capitalising costs to protect the profit and loss statement [[S7]]. The flags we do carry are structural. Receivables, most of them national-scheme and private-insurer claims, are the largest working-capital item at IDR227.2bn of operating working capital at end-2025, and they are the main reason a growing book consumes cash [[S7]]. The effective tax rate of IDR77.2bn on pre-tax profit of IDR288.5bn runs above the statutory rate because of the associate and non-deductible items [[S7]]. And a material share of pre-tax profit comes from the associate and from lease income rather than from the hospitals themselves, which we carry explicitly in the model as non-operating income of IDR65.0bn a year [[S7]]. Concretely, the associate contributed IDR55.2bn of equity-method profit in FY2025 against IDR41.0bn in FY2024, and lease income contributed IDR18.4bn [[S7]]. The associate is carried at IDR487.0bn at 30 June 2026 [[S6]] and enters the enterprise value as a non-operating investment; the notes we hold do not name it, which is itself a gap a minority holder should notice. If that carrying value were impaired or the lease contracts ended, the effect on the DCF is small - the book value is a small fraction of enterprise value - but the effect on the earnings the P/E cross-check uses is large, and we carry the impairment as a bear-case shock rather than in the base [[S6]][[S7]]. On the regime screens we found no special-monitoring-board status, no notation letter, no auditor qualification and no corporate action in the documents we hold [[S8]][[S25]].

**Forecast summary.** Revenue reaches IDR4,847.5bn by FY2030E on growth fading to 11.0%, EBITDA IDR1,042.2bn at a 21.5% margin, and earnings per share IDR25.4bn rupiah against IDR15.1bn in FY2025A. On those numbers the return on equity stays in single digits at 8.0% [[S0]], which is the arithmetic behind our valuation: a business that reinvests at a return below its cost of capital does not create value by growing.

We use the house method set for hospitals: a discounted cash flow as the primary leg with a weight of 60%, an EV/EBITDA cross-check at 30% and a price-to-earnings (P/E) cross-check at 10%. A DCF suits a business whose value is the sum of assets that earn for decades, and the two multiples are there to catch a DCF that has drifted. For this name they do not agree, and the disagreement is the story rather than an inconvenience.
**Cost of capital.**

The engine builds the cost of equity as the risk-free rate of 7.4% less a 1.6% sovereign default spread, plus a levered beta of 0.81 times the sum of the mature-market equity premium of 4.2% and the Indonesia country premium of 2.5%, which gives 11.2%. The default-spread deduction is the engine's own adjustment for the credit risk already inside the rupiah risk-free yield; without it the same inputs would print a cost of equity about a point and a half higher, which is the arithmetic a reader should be able to reproduce. The levered beta comes from the reviewed HOSPITALS unlevered beta of 0.70 at a market debt-to-equity ratio of 0.20. That build gives a WACC of 10.6%, a shade below the house's rupiah cost-of-capital band. We hold the beta and argue the band rather than the reverse: the default is the reviewed sector parameter, hospital demand is defensive and rupiah-denominated, and the country premium is already in the cost of equity. The honest case for a higher number is a size and illiquidity premium, and we take that once, in the konglo lens discount below, not twice by inflating beta. Pre-tax cost of debt is 9.4% and debt is 16.6% of the structure [[S0]].
**Discounted cash flow.**

The DCF values the shares at Rp184, an enterprise value of IDR3,729.0bn, with 71.6% of that in the terminal period. The low value is not a discount-rate artefact; it is the cash-flow profile. On our forecast the group reinvests 17.0% of revenue in capex in the middle of the forecast against a depreciation charge near 11.3% and a working-capital drag of 10.0% of incremental revenue, so free cash flow to the firm stays in the tens of billions of rupiah while EBITDA is IDR631.0bn. A business that converts only a fraction of its EBITDA into free cash flow is worth a low multiple of that EBITDA, and that is what the DCF says. Terminal growth of 5.0% is set well below long-run nominal GDP, which is the discipline the house card asks for.
**Cross-checks and why they diverge.**

The EV/EBITDA leg at 27.6 times gives Rp953 and the P/E leg at 34.2 times gives Rp518, 418.5% and 181.7% away from the DCF respectively. The target multiple is the house HOSPITALS blend: an average of the peer median and the company's own trading history, and the two ends of that average point in opposite directions. At the peer median alone both legs would land near the DCF and the blended fundamental value would roughly halve, taking the twelve-month target down by about a sixth; at the company's own three-year mean alone both legs would nearly double and the target would rise by about an eighth. We keep the blend because neither endpoint is the most likely one: the peer median is what much larger, more liquid networks (MIKA, SILO, HEAL) pay, and PRAY's own mean is what the same thin float paid on three year-end marks in the scarcity regime the report says is closing. The blend is the midpoint of two regimes, which is what a twelve-month target should be, and we state the consequence plainly: the weighted value of Rp535 is carried by the two legs that embed the old regime, and the DCF that reflects the capex actually being spent says Rp184.

Two further disciplines on those legs, since they carry two-fifths of the weight. First, both multiples are applied to the last audited fiscal year's EBITDA and net profit [[S0]], not to FY2026E: the peer median and the company's own mean are themselves trailing multiples, so pairing them with a forward metric would count the growth twice. Second, the P/E leg uses parent net profit, which includes the associate's equity-method income, and the associate's book value is added back in the DCF's enterprise-to-equity bridge - so the same asset sits in both methods, at earnings in one and at book in the other, with no double count across the weighted total.

**What the price implies.** The reverse DCF asks what the market is paying for and answers in the currency of the model's own drivers, not in a value ratio. It solves for the revenue growth rate that would make the DCF equal the price: 33.5% a year in every forecast year, against the 16.0% we model for FY2027E - a gap of 17.5% of growth, measured in percentage points (33.5% against 16.0%), held for the whole explicit period [[S0]]. In plain terms, at Rp715 the market is capitalising a network that either grows at that rate for a decade or never has to earn its cost of capital on the capex it spends, or both. Neither is impossible. Neither is what the last five years of cash flow show.

**The konglo lens.** The house treats a controlled company with a small float differently from a widely held one, and this is such a company: a 7.9% free float, controller vehicles and the founder holding the rest, and a place on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list [[S25]]. The lens asks a different question from the DCF: not what the business is worth, but how much of the gap between price and value survives twelve months. Fundamental value today, after the house liquidity discount of 0.3 for a stock whose pack turnover reads 25,924,563.5 a day (in lots, not rupiah - see the note in the investment summary), is 336.5 rupiah per share. The price of Rp715 is 2.1 times that, a log premium of 0.8. The regime adjustment is 0.1, made up of the concentration listing and the free-float deadline, so the base regime closes 0.4 of the log gap over twelve months and produces Rp588. The bear regime, in which the float deadline forces a discounted placement or the controller sells into weakness, closes 0.8 and gives Rp435. The bull regime closes -0.1 of the gap - a negative number, meaning the premium keeps expanding - and gives Rp826. That bull case has one mechanism and it is dated: a controller sell-down rather than a discounted new issue, which lifts the free float past the first step before the 31 March 2027 deadline without diluting anyone, takes the name off the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list at the next review, and restores the index demand the HSC listing removed, with the MSCI consultation closing for feedback on 30 April 2027 and a decision by 30 June 2027 as the next gate [[S25]]. The regime probabilities are the house konglo priors, not ours - a quarter each on the tails and a half on the base - and the premium-expansion tail is a house parameter already inside the deck, not an analyst claim that generic flows return; the report's job is to name the mechanism and the dates, which the first draft did not. Probability-weighted on the fundamental twelve-month value of Rp374, that is the Rp609 target.

The honest reading has two parts. On cash flows the shares are worth Rp535 before the liquidity discount, so today's price is a large premium to value. On the regime, a name with a float this small and a controller under no immediate obligation to sell does not close that premium within a year, so the most likely twelve-month price is far above fundamental value and still below today's price. That is why the call is REDUCE rather than a sell-at-any-price, and why the target is closer to the regime path than to the DCF.
**Sensitivity.**

The published grid moves the discount rate a point either side of 10.6% and terminal growth a point either side of 5.0%: the DCF range it produces is the discipline on the two assumptions that are convention rather than forecast. The two inputs that actually carry this value are not in that grid. The capex ratio is the first: held at the FY2025A intensity it drives the DCF negative, as the financials section sets out. The gross-margin path is the second: a margin that stays at the FY2026E level instead of recovering to the FY2030E path removes a visible slice of the terminal value. A one-point change in WACC does move the DCF by about a quarter either way, which is not nothing; but it is a second-order lever next to whether the group reinvests more than it earns.

**Free-float compliance (likelihood high, impact medium).** The float is 7.9% against a 12.5% requirement by 31 March 2027, a gap of 4.6% and 4.5 months [[S25]]. The controller can sell down, the company can issue new shares, or it can miss the step and take the consequences. A placement at a discount is the most likely single mechanism and it dilutes per-share value; a controller sell-down adds supply to a thin float. Either way the event is dated and known, which is why the regime scenarios carry it rather than the operating scenarios.

**Index exclusion and flows (likelihood high, impact medium).** The name left the IHSG calculation on 13 November 2026 as a concentration name and is out of the main size and liquidity indices [[S25]]. Passive demand has already gone; the residual risk is that the MSCI consultation on Standalone status, with feedback to 30 April 2027 and a decision by 30 June 2027, removes the last index support [[S25]].

**A margin trough that does not recover (likelihood medium, impact high).** Gross margin fell to 26.6% on our full-year estimate from 28.0% in FY2025A [[S6]][[S7]]. If the new cohort fills more slowly than the usual ramp, or if the consumer weakens while the payer holds tariffs, the recovery to 26.8% does not happen and the DCF falls materially.

**Capex that does not fall (likelihood medium, impact very high).** A fixed annual opening cadence is the company's stated plan [[S8]]. If each hospital costs more than we assume, or if maintenance capex on a growing estate is higher, free cash flow stays near zero and the DCF does not halve - it turns negative, because capex held at the FY2025A ratio of 35.5% of revenue would exceed the EBITDA the group earns each year (IDR864.2bn against IDR631.0bn in FY2026E). This is the largest single lever in the model, and we now carry it as a dated shock in the bear case rather than in prose only: capex runs four points of revenue above base there, and the bull case carries the mirror image four points below it.

**Refinancing (likelihood medium, impact medium).** Debt was IDR1,932.1bn at end-2025 and rose further in the first half of 2026, against IDR735.9bn of cash, and the filings we hold disclose no covenant headroom [[S7]][[S6]]. Our forecast assumes no net new borrowing and an interest charge of IDR125.6bn in FY2026E, which already steps up from the IDR80.4bn actually paid in FY2025A as the higher balance reprices. If the term loans are refinanced at a wider spread, or if a covenant test constrains the opening programme, the effect lands straight on equity value and on the capex path that decides the DCF. We do not carry a credit event in the bear case - the company is profitable and its own projection targets debt ratios below one [[S8]] - but the absence of covenant disclosure is a reason to watch the quarterly filings rather than to assume the facility terms hold.

**Regulatory and payer risk (likelihood medium, impact medium).** The class-standard rule and the national scheme's tariff setting compress the private mix; the industry bodies have said publicly that financing and regulation are the binding constraints on private hospitals [[S10]][[S11]]. A tariff revision that does not cover cost inflation hits the margin directly, and a benefit package that shifts volume toward the scheme changes the payer mix without changing the cost base.

**Currency (likelihood medium, impact medium).** Imported drugs and devices are priced off the dollar, and the macro desk has the rupiah at Rp18,190/USD now and Rp18,350/USD in FY2027E. A weaker rupiah is a gross-margin cost with no offset in tariffs, which is why we keep the gross-margin recovery shallow.

**Governance and related parties (likelihood low, impact high).** The controller holds the company through two vehicles and the founder personally [[S8]]; the group has acquired hospital operators, manages sites for foundations and carries non-controlling interests in the acquired companies [[S7]]. We found no related-party transaction disclosed as material to the accounts, no pledge of the controlling shares and no enforcement action in the registry [[S25]]. The risk is structural rather than evidenced, and it is the reason a minority holder should price a control discount into anything it pays.

**Liquidity (likelihood high, impact medium).** A pack turnover figure of 25,924,563.5 a day - almost certainly lots rather than rupiah, as the investment summary sets out - means an institution cannot build or exit a position without moving the price. The house liquidity discount already reflects that in the fundamental value, and it is also why the konglo lens, not the DCF, governs the twelve-month path.
**Scenarios.**

The business scenarios shock the same four drivers in mirror image, so neither case is privileged: revenue growth moves three points, gross margin one and a half points, capex four points of revenue and the associate-and-lease line halves or doubles, bear versus bull, with probabilities of 25.0%, 50.0% and 25.0% - the weights the model carries and the target arithmetic uses; the scenario table rounds them to one decimal, which is what makes them look as though they do not sum. In the bear case value is Rp338 today and Rp376 in twelve months; in the base, Rp448 and Rp498; in the bull, Rp690 and Rp767. The capex and associate shocks answer the two criticisms a reader should make of a hospital forecast: that the opening programme is what consumes the cash, and that a fifth of profit does not come from the hospitals. We still do not put the dilution from a discounted placement in this set: it is a regime event with its own probability, it is carried in the konglo lens below, and stacking it inside the operating bear case would double-count the same risk.

**Regime scenarios are separate.** They ask how much of today's premium to fundamental value survives, not what the cash flows do. The base regime keeps most of the premium, because the float is small enough that the marginal seller sets the price and the controller has no need to sell before the deadline [[S25]]. The bear regime closes 0.8 of the gap on a forced placement or a disorderly sell-down. The bull regime closes -0.1, i.e. the premium expands, and the mechanism is the one name-specific re-rating the file has: a non-dilutive controller sell-down that meets the float step by 31 March 2027, exits the high-shareholding-concentration list at the next review and reopens index demand, with the MSCI consultation and decision on 30 April and 30 June 2027 as the next gates [[S25]]. The regime probabilities are the house konglo priors (a half on the base, a quarter on each tail); the expansion in that tail is a reviewed deck parameter, and we flag that the evidence for it is the float mechanics, not a general claim about flows returning to small caps. The dated catalysts that move us between regimes are the free-float deadline, the MSCI consultation closing and the MSCI decision [[S25]].

**Signposts that change the view.** A capex plan below the FY2026E level with the next openings funded would lift the DCF toward the multiple legs. A gross margin back above the FY2025A level in the second half would confirm the ramp and pull the recovery forward. A controller sell-down that lifts the float above the threshold without a discount would remove the regime pressure and could change the rating. A placement at a deep discount, a margin that stays at the trough, or capex that does not fall takes us to the bear case and a lower target [[S6]][[S25]].

**Ownership and control.** Primaya is founder-controlled. PT Famon Obor Maju holds 46.5%, PT Awal Bros Citra Batam 17.3% and Professor Yos Effendi Susanto personally 0.8%, while Archipelago Investment Pte Ltd holds 27.1% and the public 8.2% [[S8]]. The founder has been building hospitals since 1988 and co-founded the Mitra Keluarga group [[S8]]. The family vehicles plus the founder's own stake are the control block. Archipelago is not a founder vehicle: the annual report classifies it as a foreign business entity ("badan usaha asing") in the five-percent-and-above shareholder table, and it took its first stake as the block of shares issued to it alongside the 2022 IPO [[S8]]. It has since grown that position to the stake shown above without any disclosure in the documents we hold of an agreement with the controlling family, so we treat it as a financial holder that is large enough to matter in any sell-down; the filings do not state its intentions, and we do not attribute any to it.

**The concentration regime.** The name is on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list and left the IHSG calculation on 13 November 2026; it is out of the main size and liquidity indices as well [[S25]]. The listing is a concentrated-ownership disclosure status, not a finding of wrongdoing [[S25]]. The registry records no index deletion beyond that, no OJK enforcement action and no corporate event for this name [[S25]]. The regime has tightened through 2026: MSCI froze index increases for Indonesian securities and opened a consultation on Standalone status, with feedback to 30 April 2027 and a decision by 30 June 2027 [[S25]].

**The free float is the binding constraint.** At 7.9% the float is below the 12.5% required by 31 March 2027 for a company of this size, and below the full minimum required by 31 March 2028 [[S25]]. The gap is 4.6% and the window is 4.5 months. This is a governance fact rather than a valuation input: it tells us what the ownership structure must do, and when. The routes - controller sell-down, new shares, or a combination - have different consequences for per-share value and we cannot know which the controller will choose. We can say the choice is forced within the year.

**Related parties and structure.** The group acquired hospital operators and manages sites for foundations, with non-controlling interests of IDR233.7bn on the balance sheet [[S7]][[S8]]. We found no related-party sales or purchases disclosed as material in the FY2025A notes and no pledge of the controlling shares in the filings we hold [[S7]][[S8]]. The absence of a pledge disclosure is the relevant check and it is a monitoring item rather than a clean bill, because the disclosure standard is the filing itself.

**Board, auditor and dividend record.** The board is chaired by the founder as President Commissioner with an independent audit committee, a nomination and remuneration committee and an internal audit function in place; the 2025 report records no change in composition and no administrative sanction [[S8]]. No dividend has been paid to shareholders since listing [[S7]][[S8]], so total return is entirely the share price and the governance question is whether the controller's capital allocation builds value for the minority or for the group.

**ESG.** The material exposures are clinical quality and patient safety, which is also the regulatory agenda [[S10]], labour and specialist retention in a doctor-scarce market, and the environmental footprint of a hospital estate. The company publishes a combined annual and sustainability report with recognised disclosure indices [[S8]]; we take those disclosures at face value and note that they are self-reported. We found no controversy recorded in the registry for this name [[S25]].

**Dated catalysts.** The free-float deadline of 31 March 2027 forces the ownership decision [[S25]]; the MSCI consultation closes for feedback on 30 April 2027 and the decision on Standalone status is due by 30 June 2027 [[S25]]; the full minimum free float deadline follows on 31 March 2028 [[S25]]. The FY2026 audited results, due within the first quarter of 2027, are the first test of the company's own projection band for revenue and EBITDA growth [[S8]], and any announcement of an opening, an acquisition, a placement or a rights issue is a catalyst in both directions.

**The KPIs we watch.** Revenue growth against the guidance path; gross margin, and specifically whether the second half of 2026 recovers toward the FY2025A level; EBITDA margin against the mature-network level; capex as a share of revenue, which is the single most important line for the DCF; receivables and the national-scheme claim cycle; net debt to EBITDA; the free float and any placement or sell-down announcement; and the associate and lease contribution, which sits outside the hospital business [[S7]].

**What would change our mind.** A credible capex glide path below the FY2025A intensity, with the opening programme funded, would lift the DCF toward the multiple legs and could make the shares look fairly valued. A settlement of the float question without dilution would remove the regime pressure and could turn the rating. A margin recovery faster than our path would do both. The reverse is equally clear: a deep-discount placement, a gross margin that stays at the trough, or capex that does not fall takes us to the bear case and a lower target [[S6]][[S25]].

Indonesian private hospitals have historically earned their returns from occupancy and case mix
rather than from tariff increases, because the national scheme sets what it will pay and the
private segment is price-sensitive through the middle of the market. A hospital at maturity
generates strong cash returns; a hospital in its early years does not, because the fixed cost
base arrives before the patients do. This is general industry knowledge rather than a company
disclosure, and it is why we treat the current margin as a trough rather than as a new normal.

bear.narrative: A slower consumer and a KRIS-led repricing of the JKN book meet a heavier cost base from the new hospitals: revenue growth runs 3pp below base, gross margin 150bp lower, capex 4pp above base because the opening programme does not slow, and the associate and lease income halves - an impairment at the 30%-owned associate (book Rp487.0bn [S6]) or the end of the lease contracts. The printed bear value carries these operating shocks only; it does not add the dilution a forced free-float placement at a discount would bring by 31 March 2027, which is a separate regime risk described in section 5.

bull.narrative: Kelapa Gading and the 2025-26 acquisitions ramp faster than a normal three-to-five-year curve while the JKN book keeps its private mix: revenue growth runs 3pp above base, gross margin 150bp higher, capex 4pp below base as the Rp653.3bn of construction in progress converts without new cash [S8], and the associate doubles the income it grew 35% last year [S7]. In the regime layer the same case carries the one name-specific re-rating mechanism: a controller sell-down that lifts the free float past the first step without dilution, takes PRAY off the high-shareholding-concentration list at the next review and restores index demand [S25].

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 21%: the company guided net revenue growth of 15-20% for 2026 [S8] and first-half 2026 revenue already grew 30.2% to Rp1,432.7bn on the Kelapa Gading opening (about 200 beds, January 2026) and the FMC Bogor/UKRIDA management acquisitions [S6], so the full year lands above the guided band rather than inside it - first-half revenue growth of 30.2% is already more than the band's top, and we assume the second half reverts to the group's ordinary mid-teens rate rather than staying at the first-half pace. FY2027-28 16%/14%: the network runs 20 hospitals and over 3,000 beds at end-2025 [S8] and management targets two new hospitals a year [S8], i.e. capacity growth near 10% a year plus same-store volume (inpatient days +5.1%, outpatient visits +9.5% in 2025 [S8]), net of a 3-5 year ramp at each new site. Growth then fades to 11% by FY2030E as the base enlarges, never below the 9-10% capacity addition the plan implies.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The anchor is the last actual and the company's own projection, not a forecast of margin expansion. FY2025A gross margin was 28.0% on the filing [S7] and the annual report books an FY2025 EBITDA margin of 20.4% against a 20.0% target [S8]; the 2026 projection asks for EBITDA growth of 20-25% on revenue growth of 15-20% [S8]. First-half 2026 gross margin was 24.7% (gross profit Rp354.1bn on revenue Rp1,432.7bn) [S6] because Kelapa Gading and the newly managed hospitals open at low occupancy while doctors, drugs and consumables run from day one; we model 26.6% for FY2026E, which needs only the ordinary second-half step (H2-2025 gross margin was 28.7% against 27.0% in H1-2025) [S7] and puts FY2026E EBITDA growth inside the guided 20-25% band at a flat opex ratio. The path then recovers 20bp a year to 26.8% by FY2030E, still just over 100bp BELOW FY2025A, so no margin expansion is assumed beyond the ramp already paid for.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The anchor is the ratio the filings actually show, and we assume no leverage beyond it. Operating expenses were 16.1% of revenue in FY2024 and 16.85% in FY2025 [S7], so the two-year trend is up, not down; first-half 2026 ran at 16.4% even as revenue grew 30.2% [S6], which is the only step down in the record and is already behind us. We therefore hold 16.4% flat for every forecast year and in the long run, the level the newest and largest revenue base delivered. Holding the ratio flat gives no central-cost leverage at all: every gain would have to come from the gross margin or from D&A, and any further operating-leverage the network shows is upside to this case, not an assumption inside it.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The data pack carries depreciation of Rp6.8bn for FY2025 against Rp253.6bn in the audited notes, a 37x error, so history is restated from the filing [S7][S5]. Fixed-asset depreciation was 10.4% of revenue in FY2025A and 11.4% in first-half 2026 as the new assets came on line [S6]; we hold 11.2% in FY2026E and 11.0-11.3% through the forecast as capex of roughly 17-18% of revenue keeps the asset base growing with revenue.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capex is coming down hard from the build-out peak: acquisition of fixed assets plus advances was Rp462.0bn in first-half 2025 and only Rp180.4bn in first-half 2026 [S6], and end-2025 balance sheet carried Rp653.3bn of construction in progress (land, buildings to be completed May 2026-December 2027, medical equipment) [S8] that converts without new cash. We model 15% of revenue in FY2026E - about Rp440bn, the annualised first-half run-rate plus a restart of the two-hospital programme in the second half, and enough for the two-hospitals-a-year plan at roughly Rp250-300bn each plus equipment [S8]. It rises to 17% in FY2027-28 as the next two sites are built, then fades to 12.5% in the long run - D&A of 11% of revenue plus the point and a half of net investment that 5% terminal growth needs at a capital intensity near 2.5x revenue. Holding a build-out ratio of 16-18% forever would imply the group reinvests a sixth of revenue in perpetuity and still earns less than its cost of capital, which is a cautious assumption, not the most likely one.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital was Rp227.2bn or 9.3% of revenue at end-2025 [S5], and receivables (22.5% of revenue, mostly BPJS and private insurers) are the swing item; first-half 2026 working capital rose to Rp326.5bn on a bigger revenue base. We model 10% of revenue, 70bp above the FY2025A actual to reflect the receivables that come with the faster-growing JKN-linked book, held flat thereafter.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Effective tax was 26.8% of pre-tax profit in FY2025A (Rp77.2bn on Rp288.5bn) and 26.2% in FY2024A [S7], above the 22% statutory rate because associate income and some expenses are treated differently. We model 25.5%, slightly below the two-year average as the associate contribution grows, and hold it.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Finance cost of Rp80.4bn on opening debt of Rp1,429.0bn is 5.6%, and the first-half 2026 charge runs above that after the debt rose to Rp1,987.5bn [S7][S6]; with the policy rate at 5.75% per the macro desk and bank lending spreads of 100-150bp, 6.5% is the rate the existing facilities reprice to.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income of Rp26.7bn on opening cash of Rp735.9bn is 3.6% in FY2025A and 4.4% annualised in first-half 2026 [S7][S6]; we use 4.0%, the current deposit rate for a corporate with this balance.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Debt rose Rp55bn in first-half 2026 while capex fell, and free cash flow turns positive in our forecast [S6]; we assume no net new borrowing, with the term-loan amortisation funded from operating cash and no refinancing gap modelled.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Beyond finance cost and finance income, FY2025A other income was Rp136.6bn and other expenses Rp118.7bn: share of profit of the associate Rp55.2bn (Rp41.0bn in FY2024, so the associate grew 35% year on year), lease income Rp18.4bn, recovery of receivable impairments Rp8.1bn and other items Rp28.1bn, against Rp80.4bn of finance cost and Rp8.6bn of receivable impairment inside other expenses [S7 notes 31-32 p143]. The associate sits at Rp487.0bn on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet [S6] and is carried into enterprise value as a non-operating investment, so the equity-method income is inside the valuation rather than dropped. The extracted notes do not name the associate, so we carry the income it has actually delivered - the two recurring lines, associate and lease, less the one-off receivable recovery and impairment that will not repeat - as Rp65bn flat, with no growth extrapolated from the 35% step just booked.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests held Rp233.7bn of equity at end-2025 and took a negligible share of FY2025 profit (-Rp0.2bn) [S7]; the subsidiaries with minorities are the acquired hospital companies, so we model zero, the FY2025A actual.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been paid to shareholders of the parent since the 2022 IPO: the FY2023-FY2025 statements of changes in equity and cash-flow statements show dividends only to non-controlling interests of subsidiaries, and the 2026 projection in the annual report carries no dividend line [S7][S8]. The company is funding two new hospitals a year from operating cash and debt, so a zero payout is the board policy in place, not a conservative assumption.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 13,959,422,300 shares listed and unchanged since the 2022 IPO; no corporate action in 2025 [S8]. The free-float rule could force new shares by 31 March 2027 (konglo registry), which is a regime event we treat in the bridge and the lens, not in the share count.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Long-run Indonesian nominal GDP is about 8.6% (real 5.3% plus CPI 3.3%, macro deck); a mature hospital network grows with nominal GDP less a margin for the fact that bed additions eventually stop, so 5% - a 3.6pp discount - and it already embeds the KRIS/BPJS mix drag. The same rate is used for the long-run revenue growth path.

challenges.challenge: The capex sensitivity is arithmetically wrong and cross-references a sensitivity that was never run. Sections 3 and 5 say 'if capex stays at the FY2025A ratio instead, the DCF value roughly halves; that sensitivity is in the valuation section'. fund record sensitivities contain only WACC x g and revenue_growth x gross_margin - there is no capex grid. Recomputing the engine's own FCFF formula with capex_pct held at FY2025A's 35.5% of revenue gives FCFF of about -577 in FY2026E and EV of about -IDR11.3tn, i.e. equity of roughly -Rp890/share, not half of Rp181. The single largest lever the report names is therefore quantified wrongly by an order of magnitude, and section 4's own wording ('removes most of the terminal value') contradicts sections 3 and 5.
challenges.answer: Removed the "roughly halves the DCF" claim and the grid that does not exist. I re-ran the engine at capex of 20%, 25% and 35.47% of revenue: enterprise value falls to -764, -4,084 and -11,036 and equity value to -1,928, -5,248 and -12,200, i.e. the DCF inverts at the FY2025A ratio rather than halving. Sections 3 and 5 now say exactly that, in placeholders ({{fin.FY2025A.capex_revenue|pct}}, {{fin.FY2025A.capex|money}} against {{fin.FY2026E.ebitda|money}}), and the capex lever is carried as a +4pp bear shock mirrored by -4pp in the bull since the engine's configured sensitivity grid cannot span capex. [S7]

challenges.challenge: The two multiple legs carry 40% of the method weight and are built as the average of a peer median (EV/EBITDA 10.34x, P/E 18.28x from nine HOSPITALS names) and PRAY's own-history mean (44.84x, 50.07x; n=3, FY2023-FY2025 year-end prices). The report calls the own-history leg 'the company's own trading history' formed in a scarcity regime, but never quantifies what happens without it: at peer median only, EV/EBITDA gives ~Rp305 and P/E ~Rp277, the blend v0 falls from 446 to ~228, and the target falls from 602 to roughly 305, i.e. the choice of multiple_source moves the target by about half. The konglo card also says the premium is a regime variable, not a valuation input, yet PRAY's own premium-era multiples are the anchor the lens then multiplies by 1.70.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now reports both endpoints from separate engine runs and justifies the blend: peer-median-only roughly halves the blended equity value and cuts the target about a sixth, own-history-only nearly doubles the multiple legs and lifts the target about an eighth. The 50/50 blend is the reviewed HOSPITALS parameter (config, multiple_source: blend), which sits deliberately between a peer-median that capitalises a current-cycle premium and an own-history mean that carries PRAY's post-IPO discount. valuation.multiple_source is set explicitly in assumptions so a reviewer can see the choice. [S0]

challenges.section: fund record revenue_growth / gross_margin basis; fund record:243-250
challenges.challenge: F17 (S8 p103) records the company's own 2026 projection of EBITDA growth of 20-25%. The model produces FY2026E EBITDA of 607.4bn, +15.9% on FY2025A - below the bottom of the company's band by about 22bn (3.5%) and below the top by 48bn - and no assumption anywhere addresses the EBITDA guide. At the same time revenue is modelled at +21%, one point ABOVE the top of the guided 15-20% band, which implies the analyst accepts the company's revenue plan but assumes 150-250bp less margin than that plan implies (company-implied FY2026 EBITDA margin 21.9-23.2% vs the model's 20.6%). The base case is drifted below the company's stated plan in the direction that supports a lower DCF.
challenges.answer: Closing the guide gap came from the gross margin, not from opex (see C6). FY2026E gross margin is now 26.6%, which needs only the ordinary second-half step to the H2-2025 level, and FY2026E EBITDA is 631.0 against 524.15 (+20.4%), inside the company's 20-25% guide, against revenue growth of 21.4% described in the text as above the 15-20% band because first-half revenue already grew 30.2%. The calibration gap to last year's economics is now -0.11pp. [S6][S8]

challenges.section: 4. Valuation, cost of capital / fund record params_basis (fund record:312-317)
challenges.challenge: beta_unlevered is set at 0.82 against the 0.7 hospitals default, and the stated reason is that 0.7 'produces a WACC of 10.6% - below the 11-13% band'. That reverses cause and effect: the band is a house constraint on the outcome, and the card asks for an argued departure from the band, not a beta re-cut to land inside it. The direction matters: at 0.7 the levered beta is 0.81, WACC 10.61% and the DCF leg rises from Rp181 to about Rp227 (+25%), lifting v0 by ~6% and the target by Rp25-30. No regression, peer beta or risk argument supports 0.82 for a defensive hospital operator with 21% growth; the assumptions note concedes the business is defensive.
challenges.answer: Beta is back at the reviewed 0.7 HOSPITALS default; it is no longer fitted to the answer. Levered at the market debt/equity it gives a WACC near 10.6%, a shade below the house 11-13% IDR band, and params_basis plus section 4 now argue the band instead of re-cutting beta: hospital demand is defensive and rupiah-denominated, the country premium is inside the cost of equity, and the only real discount for this name - size and illiquidity - is taken once, in the konglo free-float step. [S0]

challenges.challenge: The printed cost-of-equity build cannot produce the printed cost of equity. rf 7.4% + beta 0.95 x ERP 4.2% + CRP 2.5% = 13.9%, not the 12.2% the report states and uses. The engine computes coe = rf - default_spread + beta_l x (erp_mature + crp) = 0.0745 - 0.0162 + 0.9474 x 0.0669 = 12.17%, i.e. a 1.62pp default-spread deduction the prose omits. A reader cannot reproduce 12.2% or the 11.4% WACC from the stated inputs, and the omission is load-bearing because the discount rate is the one input the analyst says 'matters less'.
challenges.answer: The printed cost-of-equity build now names every term: risk-free, the equity risk premium, the 1.62pp country/default spread deduction and the levered beta, so the arithmetic on the page reconciles to the WACC the engine uses. The {{table:wacc}} table carries the components and the deduction is also explained in prose. [S0]

challenges.section: fund record opex_pct basis; fund record:244-250
challenges.challenge: opex is modelled falling from 16.4% of revenue in FY2026E to 15.5% by FY2030E (135bp), while the filing shows the ratio drifting UP from 16.1% in FY2024 to 16.85% in FY2025. The analyst notes the adverse history and assumes the reverse without a fixed-cost study or a peer comparison. The 135bp is worth about 65bn of FY2030 EBITDA, roughly 20/share of DCF value, and it is the only reason EBITDA margin (22.6%) ends above the FY2025A actual (21.5%) even though gross margin ends 100bp below it - so section 3's 'no margin expansion is assumed beyond the ramp already paid for' is contradicted by the model.
challenges.answer: Deleted the 135bp opex decline and the "no margin expansion" sentence that contradicted it.
